newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt includes jobs, taxes in welfare talks.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt includes jobs, taxes in welfare talks.

text.p: The Italian government said on Thursday it would review the question of tax evasion and employment in forthcoming welfare talks which will include a review of a 1995 reform of the state pensions system.
Various working parties, to be made up of union, business and government representatives, will meet in the first half of July, Prime Minister Romano Prodi's office said in a statement.
It said the discussion groups must produce initial findings by the end of July for general negotiations.

Italy is under pressure to carry out a convincing reform of social spending -- and to shake up its pensions system -- to prove that public finances will be kept under control before the planned 1999 launch of the single European currency.
Prodi opened talks last week with Italy's three main union confederations, trade bodies and employers' group Confindustria on the controversial question of welfare and pension reform.
Under the terms of the 1995 pension deal, enacted by the then government of Lamberto Dini, a review of the reform was not due until 1998 and unions had wanted to stick to this timetable.

However the government is anxious to include the planned overhaul of pension spending in the 1998 budget, which must be presented to parliament by the end of September 1997, and forced the unions to bring the review forward.
Having conceded to Prodi on the pension issue, unions got their way in demanding that the question of both employment and tax fraud should be included in the overall negotiations.

Prodi's centre-left coalition has indicated that it wants to save some 10 trillion lire from the welfare budget next year, keeping social spending as a ratio of gross domestic product (GDP) pegged to 1996/97 levels.

Italy's trade unions agree that the welfare system, which is heavily weighted in favour of pension benefits and offers little in the way of assistance to the unemployed or families, should be re-jigged, but are against any cut in spending.
"The negotiations will be difficult," Sergio D'Antoni, the leader of Italy's second largest union, the Cisl, told reporters on Thursday. "The positions are far apart," he added.
Giorgio Fossa, the chairman of Confindustria, predicted this week that the complex negotiations would have to go on beyond the end of September.
Prodi's office gave the following timetable for the talks:
July 2 - The employment discussion group meets for first time as well as the group studying fiscal matters.
July 10 - The health and housing group meets.
The government will be represented by various ministers in each of the five working parties. -- Rome newsroom +396 6782501
